newsitem.title: USA: NYC Indep. Budget Office sees more revs than mayor.
newsitem.headline: NYC Indep. Budget Office sees more revs than mayor.

text.p: New York City's Independent Budget Office predicted Friday that tax revenues in fiscal 1998 would grow to $18.937 billion, about $35 million more than Mayor Rudolph Giuliani has estimated.

The body, which was newly created under the city charter to function like the Congressional Budget Office, said the difference stemmed from variations in the economic assumptions that it and the Giuliani Administration made.

In its first fiscal outlook, which the charter requires, Independent Budget Office also was more optimistic about fiscal 1999 revenues: it said collections would rise $62 million more than Guiliani predicted to $19.542 billion.

But the group's forecasts for 2000 and 2001 were more pessimistic. It looks for fiscal 2000 revenues to total $20.247 billion, $24 million less than the mayor. And the outlook prepared by the Independent Budget Office was markedly less rosy in 2001, as it sees collections totaling $20.894 billion -- $233 million less than the Guiliani Administration.

Noting that during most of the past two decades, the city's baseline revenue growth has lagged the local economy, the body recommended that New York City adopt the "current services" budgeting method used by Washington.
This technique is designed to project spending and revenues, assuming there are no changes in tax policy and that present spending levels continue though they are adjusted for inflation.

Douglas Criscitello, director, in prepared remarks, said the report's differing forecasts should be used as a yardstick for measuring how much proposed policies cost. "From a longer-term perspective, it is an early warning indicator capable of identifying potential future fiscal difficulties for the city."

Specifically, the group identified three main risks for the city, saying Congressional proposals to reauthorize the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act could have a major impact on its capital budget for roads and bridges. Developments outside the city's control also could affect it greatly, like an economic downturn that caused welfare spending to rise as people who lost their jobs applied for benefits and how much of its federal welfare grant Albany elects to share with the city.

While the Giuliani Administration has promised to close the Fresh Kills landfill by the end of 2001, the Department of Sanitation will have to find other ways of dealing with its garbage, which could trigger higher costs, unless the agency finds offsetting savings.
